title: Understanding the Exemptions to California's Transfer Disclosure Statement Requirement
content_html:
Most people who have bought or sold a home in California have encountered the Real Estate Transfer Disclosure Statement, commonly called the TDS. It's the form where a seller describes the condition of the property, known defects, and material facts a buyer would want before completing a purchase. But the TDS requirement isn't universal — California law carves out specific categories of transfers where the statutory disclosure statement isn't required. Understanding these exemptions matters whether you're a buyer trying to figure out what protections apply to your transaction, or a seller trying to understand your obligations.

This article walks through the major exemption categories under California law, and just as importantly, explains what these exemptions do not mean — because in most cases, an exemption from the TDS form doesn't eliminate a seller's broader duty to disclose known material defects.

What the TDS Requirement Covers

California Civil Code sets out the transfer disclosure statement requirement for sales of most residential real property of one to four units.[1] The statute also lists categories of transfers to which the TDS requirement does not apply.[2] If you'd like a broader overview of how seller disclosures work generally in California, our article on seller disclosure requirements covers the landscape beyond just the TDS form itself.

Transfers Exempt From the TDS Requirement

The statute identifies several specific circumstances under which a transfer is exempt from the TDS requirement.[2] These generally include:

  • Court-ordered transfers, such as transfers pursuant to a probate proceeding, a writ of execution, or an order of a bankruptcy court.
  • Foreclosure-related transfers, including transfers by a trustee under a deed of trust and transfers to a beneficiary of a deed of trust who has foreclosed.
  • Transfers by certain fiduciaries acting within the scope of their official duties, such as a trustee of a trust, a guardian, or a conservator.
  • Transfers between co-owners, including transfers from one co-owner to one or more other co-owners.
  • Transfers to a spouse or to a person or persons within the same family, such as transfers resulting from a divorce, legal separation, or dissolution of a domestic partnership.
  • Transfers by the Controller in connection with unclaimed property, and certain transfers between governmental entities.

Each of these categories reflects situations where the legislature determined that the transaction context — a court proceeding, a fiduciary relationship, a transfer within a family, or a governmental action — makes the standard buyer-facing disclosure form less relevant or impractical to require.

New Construction and Other Special Cases

New residential construction, where the property is being sold for the first time and is covered by a public report requirement, is treated differently under state law with respect to certain disclosure obligations. Builders and developers of new construction typically have separate disclosure obligations tied to the public report process rather than the resale TDS form. If you're weighing new construction against a resale purchase, our guide on new construction versus resale homes in Temecula Valley discusses some of these practical differences.

What an Exemption Does Not Mean

This is the point that trips up both buyers and sellers most often: being exempt from the TDS form is not the same as being exempt from disclosing known problems with a property. California law separately imposes disclosure duties tied to natural hazard zones, and other statutory and common-law obligations can still apply to a transaction even when the TDS form itself isn't required.

A seller who is exempt from completing a TDS — say, a trustee selling trust property, or a parent transferring a home to an adult child — may still need to address other disclosure items depending on the transaction, such as natural hazard disclosures. Our article on the California Natural Hazard Disclosure Statement explains that separate requirement in more detail, since it operates on its own legal basis and isn't automatically waived by a TDS exemption.

In practice, this means an exempt seller should still talk with a real estate professional or attorney about what, if anything, should be disclosed to the buyer given the specifics of the property and the transaction. An exemption from a specific statutory form is a legal technicality about which paperwork is required — it isn't a green light to withhold known, material information about a property's condition.

Why This Distinction Matters for Buyers

If you're buying a property through an exempt transfer — for example, purchasing from an estate, inheriting a home through a family transfer, or buying at a trustee's sale — it's worth understanding upfront that you may be receiving less formal disclosure documentation than you would in a typical resale. That makes independent due diligence more important, not less. A thorough home inspection and a careful review of available property records become more valuable safeguards when the standard disclosure paperwork isn't part of the transaction.

Title issues can also carry more weight in these situations, since exempt transfers often arise from probate, foreclosure, or inheritance circumstances where prior liens, disputes, or ownership questions are more likely to surface. Understanding how title insurance works and confirming a clean title search is a sensible step in any transaction, but especially one where the seller isn't required to provide the standard disclosure form.

Why This Distinction Matters for Sellers

If you believe your transaction qualifies for a TDS exemption, don't assume that means no disclosure conversation is necessary. Buyers who later discover a serious, known defect that wasn't disclosed can raise legal claims regardless of whether a TDS form was technically required, if other disclosure duties applied and weren't met. Sellers in an exempt category — trustees, executors, co-owners transferring interests, or family members transferring property — are well served by documenting what they knew about the property's condition and confirming with a professional which other disclosures, if any, still apply to their specific situation.

A Practical Starting Point

Because the exemption categories are specific and fact-dependent — turning on exactly who is transferring the property, under what legal process, and to whom — it's worth confirming exemption status with a real estate professional or attorney rather than assuming a transaction qualifies based on a general description. The consequences of misclassifying a transaction, either by skipping a required disclosure or by over-disclosing in a way that creates confusion, are avoidable with a short conversation early in the transaction.

For sellers navigating an unusual or exempt transfer, and for buyers trying to understand what documentation to expect, working through these questions early — ideally before a purchase agreement is signed — tends to make for a smoother closing.
